title: How to take notes in a case interview (a simple page layout)
description: A practical way to lay out your paper in a case interview so you can find the goal, your structure and the numbers when you need them.
hook: Notes sound like a small thing, but messy notes are behind many lost cases. Twenty minutes in, you need the client's goal or a number from the prompt, and you cannot find it. A simple, consistent page layout fixes that, and it frees your head to think.
body:
A layout that works

  • Page 1, top: the client's goal, in a box, with any number and deadline. "Restore profit to £10M within 2 years."
  • Page 1, below: key facts from the prompt in short bullets. Circle anything surprising.
  • Page 2: your structure, drawn large, landscape if it helps. Leave space under each branch to add findings later.
  • Page 3 onwards: one page per calculation or chart. Write the question at the top, then the working, then the answer with units, circled.

Small habits that help

  • Write numbers with units: "£4.5M a year", not "4.5".
  • Use abbreviations you will recognise later: Rev, Cost, Cust, Mkt, Comp.
  • Number your pages so you can say "on page two I noted..."
  • Turn the structure page towards the interviewer when you present it. It helps them follow you.

For online interviews

You will usually still use paper. Hold your structure up to the camera if it helps, or describe it clearly. Some candidates like a whiteboard behind them for the structure; use whatever lets you think calmly.

Before the end

Glance at your goal box before you give your recommendation. It is the simplest way to make sure your answer matches the question that was actually asked.
outro: Small things like this add up. Try it in your next practice case and notice how it changes the conversation.
